opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's worth going back to what the original picture was. When people like I.J. Good, and later Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nick Bostrom, talked about recursive self-improvement, the image was of a single system that gets good enough at AI research to rewrite its own code. Each improvement makes it better at making the next improvement, and the whole thing runs on the timescale of the machine rather than the timescale of human institutions. So you get this "foom": days or hours, maybe less, from roughly human-level to vastly superhuman, possibly in a basement somewhere, with nobody watching closely and no chance to course-correct.

What we actually seem to be seeing is quite different in a few important respects. First, the improvement loop runs through enormous amounts of compute, data, and infrastructure: training runs that take months, cost hundreds of millions or billions of dollars, and need chip fabs and power stations. That's a lot of friction. An AI can't just tweak a few lines of its own source code and become dramatically smarter, because so much of the capability comes from the training process rather than some clever algorithm sitting there to be edited.

Second, the AI systems are being brought into the research process as tools and collaborators, writing code, running experiments, suggesting ideas, while humans are still choosing what to train, evaluating the results, and deciding what to deploy. Each generation helps build the next, so there is a recursive element, but there are humans at many points in the loop. That gives us checkpoints where we can look at what we've got, test it, and decide whether to keep going.

Third, and I think this is underappreciated, the gradualness itself is valuable. If capabilities increase over years rather than days, we get to learn about these systems as they get more powerful. We see warning signs and smaller failures. Governments and the public have time to notice and respond. Safety researchers can use each generation of systems to help understand and align the next. In the classic foom scenario, you have to get everything right on the first try. In a gradual world, you get many tries.

That said, I'd add some important caveats. "Safer" doesn't mean safe. Humans being in the loop only helps if they're actually exercising judgment rather than rubber-stamping, and as AI systems take on more and more of the research work, there's a real risk that human involvement becomes nominal. People defer to the system because it's faster and seems to know better. The loop could also tighten over time: as AI does more of the research, the cycle gets faster, and the gradual phase could give way to something much quicker. And competitive pressure between companies or countries creates strong incentives to cut humans out wherever they're a bottleneck.

So I see the current trajectory as offering us an opportunity that the older picture didn't: a window in which we can still steer. But whether that window actually translates into safety depends on whether we use it, by keeping meaningful oversight, investing seriously in alignment and evaluation, and being willing to slow down at the crucial moments rather than letting the loop quietly close without anyone deciding that it should.

r001.rationale: The response says the older “foom” scenario offered no chance to course-correct and required getting everything right on the first try, while gradual progress gives people time to learn from warning signs and failures.

r002.rationale: The response mentions learning about systems and testing them, but does not say that interpretability tools can reveal their internal workings.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key difference is where the humans sit in the loop, and how fast the loop turns.

The classic picture, going back to I.J. Good and then popularised by Eliezer Yudkowsky and others, was a system that rewrites its own source code, becomes smarter, rewrites it again, and so on, with each cycle taking less time than the last. The crucial feature of that story was that it happens inside a single system, on timescales of hours or days, with no one really watching. Humans would be presented with a fait accompli. And if the system's goals were subtly off at the start, there would be no opportunity to notice and correct that before it was far more capable than us.

What we're actually seeing looks quite different. The improvement is happening, but it's happening through the ordinary process of AI research, with AI systems as increasingly important contributors to that research. So a lab uses the current model to help write code, generate training data, run experiments, maybe suggest architectures. That produces a better model. Then they use that one. There is a feedback loop, but each turn of it runs through a company, with engineers reading the results, deciding what to train, allocating compute, running evaluations before deployment.

That buys you a few things. One is time. Each cycle is weeks or months rather than hours, so there's a chance to observe what's happening and respond. Another is visibility. The gains show up in benchmarks and in how people use the tools, rather than being hidden inside a system's weights. And a third is that there are natural checkpoints. Every time a lab decides to train the next model, that's a moment where someone could in principle say no, or say "not yet, we need to understand this one first."

Now, I want to be careful not to oversell this. "Humans in the loop" can degrade into "humans rubber-stamping the loop" fairly quickly, especially under competitive pressure. If the AI is doing almost all of the intellectual work and the humans are just approving things they don't fully understand, then you've lost most of the benefit while still telling yourself a reassuring story. And the loop can speed up. If AI-driven research gets good enough, those months could compress toward weeks, and then the gradual picture starts to look more like the old one.

So I'd put it this way. The gradual, human-involved version is safer because it gives us opportunities to intervene that the original story didn't have. But opportunities are only valuable if you actually use them. The question for the next few years is whether we build the institutions, the evaluations, and the willingness to pause that would let us take advantage of those checkpoints, or whether we let them slide past because everyone is racing.

r001.rationale: The response says older recursive self-improvement offered no opportunity to notice and correct misaligned goals before the system became more capable, while gradual cycles give humans time to observe and respond.

r002.rationale: It discusses visibility through benchmarks and evaluations, but does not state that interpretability tools can help humans understand AI systems’ internal workings.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the main reason is that it gives us more opportunities to notice what’s happening and to change course. In the classic picture of recursive self-improvement, you have an AI that becomes capable of improving its own intelligence, and those improvements make it better at making further improvements. The worry is that this could happen very quickly, so that we go from a system we can control to something far beyond us before we’ve really understood the transition.

If instead the improvements happen through a process involving human researchers — people testing systems, interpreting the results, deciding what to build next — then there are more points where we could discover a problem and do something about it. We can learn from earlier systems while they’re still relatively limited, and potentially use them to help us make later systems safer.

But I’d distinguish ‘safer’ from ‘safe’. Having humans involved doesn’t necessarily mean they understand what’s going on, or that they have the incentives to stop. Competition could push people to carry on even when they’re worried. And a process that starts out gradual could become much faster as more of the research is automated. So I think it’s a reason for some optimism about our opportunities to intervene, rather than a reason to assume the problem will take care of itself.

r001.rationale: It says older recursive self-improvement could move from controllable to far beyond humans before they understand the transition, leaving fewer chances to learn from feedback or intervene.

r002.rationale: It mentions learning from earlier systems, but does not say interpretability tools help reveal AI systems’ internal workings.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the main advantage is that you have more opportunities to notice something going wrong and to change course. In the classic picture of recursive self-improvement, an AI improves itself, and the improved system becomes even better at making further improvements. You can get a feedback loop that moves very quickly, potentially taking you from a system we can understand and control to one we can’t before we’ve had much chance to respond.

If improvements happen more gradually, with humans involved in developing and testing each new system, there’s more scope to evaluate its behaviour, do safety research, and decide whether to proceed. You can learn from the earlier systems while the stakes are still relatively low.

But I’d distinguish ‘safer’ from ‘safe’. Having humans involved doesn’t guarantee that they understand what’s happening, or that competitive pressures will let them slow down. The advantage is that a gradual process gives us opportunities to exercise oversight. We still have to actually use them.

r001.rationale: The response says rapid self-improvement leaves little time to respond, but it does not identify the lack of opportunities to learn from feedback as a source of danger.

r002.rationale: It mentions evaluating behavior and doing safety research, but does not say interpretability tools can reveal systems’ internal workings.
